sense: doing something again and again to get better

evidence: Cic. Lael. 17: egetque exercitātiōne nōn parvā
Sen. Ep. 83.4: vidē quid exercitātiō cotīdiāna prōficiat
terms.comment: Practice of any skill, not only of the body: exercitātiō dīcendī (Cic. Brut. 331, Lewis & Short). Traupman 258 gives Exercitātiō optima magistra est for “practice makes perfect”.
With what is trained as object (memoriam, vōcem), or sē exercēre, to practise.
Of rehearsing what one will say or perform.

terms.gloss: practice; the skill that comes of it
evidence: Plin. Ep. 6.29.4: ūsum et esse et habērī optimum dīcendī magistrum
Tac. A. 2.55 (Lewis & Short: post-Augustan, not in Cicero or Caesar)

phrases.latin: cumque ita balbus esset, ut ejus ipsīus artis, cui studēret, prīmam litteram nōn posset dīcere, perfēcit meditandō, ut nēmō plānius esse locūtus putārētur
phrases.english: and though he stammered so badly that he could not say the first letter of the very art he was studying, by practising he came to be thought the clearest speaker of all

phrases.latin: Nec mē praeterit ūsum et esse et habērī optimum dīcendī magistrum; videō etiam multōs parvō ingeniō litterīs nūllīs, ut bene agerent agendō cōnsecūtōs.
phrases.english: I know well that practice is, and is held to be, the best teacher of speaking; I see, too, many men of small talent and no learning who have learned to plead well by pleading.

phrases.latin: At memoria minuitur. crēdō, nisi eam exerceās
phrases.english: ‘But the memory weakens.’ No doubt, if you don’t exercise it

sources: Lewis & Short: exercitatio · Lewis & Short: exerceo · Lewis & Short: meditor · Lewis & Short: usus
